answers.flag: Option C also lowers the read capacity of the nightly report on the base table (the stream copy holds only open orders), so a careful candidate can defend it, and only the 'MOST cost-effective' tie-breaker (extra table, Lambda and write costs) separates it from B; the stem also gives no hint of how the new attribute reaches existing orders.

case.label: C
case.text: A Lambda function on the stream copies each open order into a small second table, and the report scans that table, so the Scan no longer reads the large base table at all. This removes the whole read cost of the report from the base table, at least as much as a GSI query does. It also avoids adding a GSI that needs its own capacity in provisioned mode. The stem names no cost limit on Lambda or on a second table, so C meets 'reduce the read capacity' and a careful reader could defend it. Also, the phrases 'a few seconds old' and 'few orders are open' point straight at D and B.

case.label: A
case.text: One new item per vote spreads the writes over many partition key values, so the single-item write limit no longer applies and the throttling stops. The stem gives no limit on read cost, and a Scan with a filter on the contest ID does return the correct total. A candidate who ignores the once-per-second read of the total could defend A. Its weakness is that a Scan reads the whole table each second, but the stem states that cost only indirectly.

case.label: D
case.text: Splitting a recording into parts stored as items under the call ID keeps everything in DynamoDB, so the application finds the recording from the call without a second service and keeps one consistency and access model. Each part fits the item size limit, so D is technically feasible. The stem says only 'MOST cost-effective' and does not give prices, so a candidate who does not weigh DynamoDB storage and request cost against S3 could defend D. C is ruled out only by the item size limit, which the stem does not state as a number; the several-MB size is the only cue.

answers.flag: Option B (a TransactWriteItems with a Put conditioned on a version attribute) also detects the conflict, so the key rests on the 'MOST cost-effective' tie-breaker (transactional writes use more write capacity than a conditional PutItem), which the stem does not spell out.

case.label: B
case.text: A TransactWriteItems call with one Put action and a condition on the version attribute rejects the write when another agent changed the item first, so the second agent gets an error and reloads the profile. That meets every stated requirement. The stem never says that the application may not use transactions or gives a capacity budget, so B is a correct way to detect the conflict. C is the same idea with a plain conditional PutItem. Only the cost wording separates them.
